record.original_question: In dark-atom dark matter models, stable particles with negative even electric charge −2n are generated in excess over their antiparticles and bind with n primordial helium-4 nuclei into neutral, nuclear-interacting atom-like states such as Bohr-like OHe for n = 1 or Thomson-like XHe for n > 1. How do these dark-atom species evolve after Big Bang nucleosynthesis, including whether XHe binding in a helium-rich medium produces anomalous isotopes and how the Bose-Einstein nature of alpha particles affects that evolution?

evidence.quote: The dark atom hypothesis assumes existence of stable particles with negative even electric charge −2n. Such particles should be generated in excess over their antiparticles and bind with n primordial helium-4 nuclei, created in Big Bang Nucleosynthesis, in neutral nuclear interacting atom like states.

Evolution of these species formed in the period of Big Bang Nucleosynthesis is the open problem of dark atom scenario. XHe atoms are formed in the medium enriched by free helium nuclei and their binding with XHe can lead to production of anomalous isotopes, which is now the object of our thorough investigation. The role of the Bose-Einstein nature of α particles is of particular interest in this investigation.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a dark-matter model in which there exist stable elementary particles carrying negative even electric charge −2n (n a positive integer), produced in the early universe with a cosmological excess over their antiparticles. After Big Bang nucleosynthesis, each such particle binds with n primordial helium-4 (alpha) nuclei to form a neutral, nuclear-interacting atom-like bound state:

• For n = 1, a Bohr-like atom OHe consisting of one doubly-charged particle and one He-4 nucleus.
• For n > 1, a Thomson-like atom XHe consisting of one charge −2n particle and n He-4 nuclei, in which the nuclei lie inside the Bohr radius of the heavy charged particle so that the binding is described in the Thomson (oscillator) approximation rather than the Bohr (point-Coulomb) approximation.

The surrounding medium just after Big Bang nucleosynthesis contains a substantial abundance of free He-4 nuclei, which are spin-0 bosons obeying Bose–Einstein statistics.

Determine the post-nucleosynthesis cosmological evolution of the OHe and XHe populations. In particular:

(a) Derive the thermal, kinetic, and chemical evolution of OHe and XHe from the epoch of their formation through recombination, including the rates of formation, dissociation, and elastic/inelastic interactions with the ambient plasma.

(b) For XHe (n > 1), determine whether the capture of additional free He-4 nuclei from the helium-rich medium onto an XHe state can occur, and, if so, compute the resulting abundance of anomalous (super-)heavy isotopes that would survive to the present epoch and compare with terrestrial and astrophysical bounds on anomalous isotopes.

(c) Quantify the effect of the Bose–Einstein nature of the alpha particles—i.e. stimulated capture and the symmetry of the multi-alpha bound state wavefunction—on the binding energies, capture cross sections, and final abundances obtained in (a)–(b).
artifact.status_search_result: The question of the post-BBN evolution of OHe/XHe dark atoms, including XHe binding in a helium-rich medium and the role of Bose–Einstein statistics of alpha particles, is explicitly identified as an open problem under active investigation by proponents of the dark-atom scenario. Recent works by Khlopov and collaborators (2023–2025) continue to describe this evolution as unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Open questions of BSM Cosmology
status_evidence.snippet: Evolution of these species formed in the period of Big Bang Nucleosynthesis is the open problem of dark atom scenario.
